items.answer: Coral polyp
items.markingKey: Coral polyp: a small marine animal that secretes a calcium carbonate skeleton; colonies build reefs. [1]

items.stem: Explain the conditions needed for coral reef growth.
items.answer: Warm water (above about 18 °C, optimum 23-29 °C); clear, shallow, well-lit water (less than about 25 m); salinity about 32-35‰; low sediment; wave action bringing oxygen and nutrients; a solid base.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per condition [4]

items.stem: Explain the relationship between corals and zooxanthellae.
items.answer: Symbiosis: algae photosynthesise and supply up to 90% of the coral’s food and its colour; the coral provides shelter, carbon dioxide and nutrients; stress causes the coral to expel the algae (bleaching).

items.stem: Ana argues that temperature is the most important factor controlling the distribution of coral reefs. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: Reefs are limited to waters above 18 °C, explaining their tropical distribution and their absence on coasts with cold currents. Against: Light and depth, salinity, sediment from rivers, a suitable base and wave action control local distribution (none at the mouth of the Amazon); sea-level history matters for reef types. Conclusion: Temperature sets the broad latitudinal limits, but local distribution depends on light, sediment and salinity.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “coral polyp”?
options: A reef separated from the mainland by a wide, deep lagoon, such as the Great Barrier Reef.
A reef growing close to the shore of a landmass, separated from it by a narrow, shallow lagoon or none at all.
Single-celled algae living in coral tissue that photosynthesise and supply the coral with food.
A small marine animal that secretes a calcium carbonate skeleton; colonies build reefs.
items.answer: A small marine animal that secretes a calcium carbonate skeleton; colonies build reefs.

items.stem: A student writes: “Coral reefs are found mainly on the west coasts of continents in the tropics.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Cold currents and upwelling make tropical west coasts too cool; reefs are mainly on east coasts.

items.stem: Compare fringing and barrier reefs.
items.answer: Fringing reefs grow close to the shore with little or no lagoon; barrier reefs lie further offshore, separated by a wide, deep lagoon; barrier reefs are larger and often older.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Compare fringing and barrier reefs. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Coral reefs support about a quarter of marine species.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Fringing reefs grow close to the shore with little or no lagoon; barrier reefs lie further offshore, separated by a wide, deep lagoon; barrier reefs are larger and often older. (b) Correct. They cover under 1% of the ocean floor but are very biodiverse.

items.stem: Explain Darwin’s subsidence theory of atoll formation.
items.answer: A fringing reef grows around a volcanic island; the island slowly subsides; the coral grows upwards at a similar rate, so the reef becomes separated from the shrinking island by a lagoon (barrier reef); when the island sinks below sea level, a ring-shaped atoll remains.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage [4]

items.stem: A borehole on an atoll similar to Bikini Atoll, Marshall Islands passes through 905 m of shallow-water reef limestone before reaching volcanic basalt. The oldest reef limestone is about 54 million years old. Reef corals can grow upwards at about 5 mm per year. Explain why reefs have not always kept up with sea-level change.
items.answer: Rapid post-glacial sea-level rise (up to 10-20 mm a year at times) and cooling or poor conditions slowed growth; some reefs drowned to form guyots.

items.stem: Explain the arguments for and against the view that Darwin’s theory provides a complete explanation of the formation of atolls.
items.answer: For: Subsidence of volcanic islands with upward reef growth explains the sequence of fringing reef, barrier reef and atoll; supported by Enewetak drilling and plate tectonics. Against: It does not explain the shape and depth of lagoons or recent features, which reflect glacial sea-level changes (Daly); some reefs grow on antecedent platforms (Murray). Conclusion: Darwin’s theory explains the origin of most atolls, but a complete explanation needs glacial sea-level change as well.

items.stem: Explain the evidence that supports Darwin’s theory.
items.answer: Boreholes such as Enewetak show thick reef limestone over volcanic basement; shallow-water coral fossils at depth show subsidence; guyots; plate tectonics explains subsidence of cooling oceanic crust.

items.stem: Explain how climate change threatens coral reefs.
items.answer: Higher sea temperatures cause bleaching and mortality; ocean acidification reduces calcification; stronger cyclones damage reefs; sea-level rise may outpace growth in some places.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per threat [4]

items.stem: Explain the local human threats to coral reefs.
items.answer: Overfishing and destructive fishing (blast, cyanide); pollution and sediment from farming and deforestation; coastal development and dredging; tourism damage (anchors, trampling); coral mining.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per threat [4]

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that global threats are more serious than local threats to coral reefs.
items.answer: For: Warming causes repeated mass bleaching (Great Barrier Reef 2016-2024); acidification reduces calcification; these cannot be managed locally. Against: Local threats (overfishing, run-off, coastal development, blast fishing in Indonesia) are severe and immediate in many places and reduce resilience to warming; they can be managed. Conclusion: Global warming is the greatest long-term threat, but local pressures determine whether reefs can survive it.

items.answer: Not correct. Corals can recover if temperatures fall soon enough, but prolonged stress kills them.

items.stem: Explain how reefs can be managed sustainably.
items.answer: Marine protected areas with zoning; controls on run-off and sewage; fishing limits; mooring buoys and visitor education; coral gardening and restoration; reducing global emissions.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Marine protected areas can increase fish catches in surrounding waters.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Protected stocks grow and spill over into fished areas.
